catalog_quote: ... Sebei are long or short. In addition to these two phonemic degrees of length, there are also extra-long vowels, which are non-phonemic. These occur optionally in noun forms with the thematic suffix (see Section 2.3) ... three degrees of length: long, "half-long," and short. The first two of these are assigned to the long "Chroneme," "half-long" being explained as "due to shift in stress." Since stress does not appear to be phonemic, but seems rather an effect of length plus high tone, this is presumably what Tucker and Bryan intend to convey by that statement. This assumption is supported by some of the words written with a "half-long" symbol: the Kipsigis stem for "hand" is written e:(y) (long) in isolation, e. new_statements.rule_in_words: Sebei (Kupsabiny) is a tone language (three level tones in Montgomery's analysis; five tones incl. contours in Kawachi 2015/2016) with contrastive vowel length; stress is not phonemic -- perceived prominence is a by-product of a long vowel carrying high tone, so there is no positional word-stress rule. Rottland 1982 says the same for Kalenjin generally: no phonemic stress, phonetic prominence always on non-low-toned syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Montgomery's remark is made while reinterpreting Tucker & Bryan's 'half-long' vowels ('shift in stress') as length dissimilation before a suffix with long vowel + high tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology of nouns/verbs in citation and suffixed forms; statement obtained via verbatim Google Books snippet chain (dissertation has no preview), so surrounding context beyond the quoted sentences was not seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Montgomery 1966 and O'Brien & Cuypers 1975 describe 'Sebei' = Kupsabiny/Kupsapiny of Sebei (Kapchorwa) District, Uganda = kups1238; Kawachi treats Kenyan Sabaot (saba1262-type variety) as a mutually intelligible dialect of the same language but his data are Ugandan Kupsapiny. Rottland 1982 sec. 5.1.3.2 is a statement about Kalenjin as a whole (his own data include Sapiny), not Kupsabiny-specific.
